*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Topic structure

Use the same structure across topics to make them more consistent.

## Example

Figure 1 shows a screenshot of the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/) topic, that follows the structure.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Structure-example-1024x861.png?resize=1024%2C861&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Example of a topic that is structured using the guidelines

## 1. Overview

The procedure and cases are presented automatically with photos, names, and short descriptions.

## 2. Introduction

Structure of the introduction page:

- **Authors**
- **Introduction**: Introduce the topic/procedure/technique/diagnosis
- **Definitions**: List terms and their definitions
- **Background**: History and year of first time performed surgery with reference
- **References**

## 3. Anatomy

Structure of the anatomy page:

- **Authors**
- **Standard anatomic composition**: E.g. the breast or flap
- **Blood supply**
- **Nerves** that should be identified and spared during the operation
- **Muscles** used for flap bulk
- **References**

For anatomy pages use drawn illustrations.

## 4. Subtopics: The theoretical background and patophysiology for the diagnosis, grades of disease or calculation.

May be several menubars in larger chapters as burns, breast surgery, melanoma or facial flaps.

The subtopics are all the theoretical parts of the topic which are not surgical procedures or cases, which should also be organized and well structured in the menu to the left.

- **Authors**
- Theoretical description of the suptopic including patophysiology, grades of disease (eg burns degree 1-3) or calculation (eg burns calculation of burnt % of TBSA) with drawn illustrations. See examples below.
- In smaller topics the patophysiology of the disease is descriped.
- **References**

### Examples for Subtopics

- **The Topic Instruments**

- Forceps

- The different kinds of forceps
- How to hold a forceps
- How to use a forceps

- Needle holder (driver)

- The different kinds of needle holders
- How to hold a needle holder
- How to use the the needle holder – the cremiere, placement of needle, etc (See also sutures)

- Etc

- **The topic Surgery Preparation**

- Surgical scrub

- Short description of background and reason to perform surgical scrub
- Description (numbered) how to perform scrub
- Video

- Sterile gloves

- Short description of types, sizes, latex vs non-latex, double-layer
- Short historic background
- Description how to put on gloves
- Video

- Etc

- **The topic Basic Surgical Technique**
- Local anesthesia

- Short description of historic background and types of local anesthesia
- How to fill up the syringe
- Description How to do local infiltration
- Video

- Surgical incision

- How to hold the knife
- Video

- Etc

- **The topic:** **Pre-OP Assesment**
- Introduction
- Aim and Background
- Medical History (More illustrations!)
- Review of Organ Systems (hedder det det?)
- Patient Examination (God ide med illustrationer. Måske blot flere normal body illustrations?)
- Plan and conclusions

- **The topic Skin Cancer the subtopics are:**

- Patophysiology of skin cancers
- Patient history and presentation

- Basal Cell Carcinoma

- Patophysiology
- Photo examples
- Treatment and surgical margins
- Link to Excision of facial tumors in the bottom

- Squamous cell carcinoma

- etc

- Merkel Cell Carcinoma

- etc

- Malignant adnexal tumors
- Pre-cancerous lesions

**The Topic: Excision of Facial tumors**

- Introduction, Background and definitions
- Anatomy

- Resting Skin Tension Lines

- Nerves

- Arteria

- Patient presentation
- Pre-operative considerations and information
- Procedure
- Scalp

- Pre-operative considerations
- Illustrations
- Excision on scalp (step-by-step procedure)
- Cases with description of photos

- Front

- etc

- Eyelid
- Nose
- Etc
- Post-operative care

- **The topic: Burns (The design of the whole chapter) is:**

- Introduction with background, definitions
- Anatomy
- Patophysiology of burns

- Local skin response
- Systemic response

- Assesment of Burn degrees

- 1st degree (Epidermal)
- 2nd degree (Dermal)
- 3rd degree (Subdermal)

- Calculating burn size

- Rule of nines
- Rule of hand
- [http://www.burn-app.com](http://www.burn-app.com) (Burn Calculator)

- Indication for referral to burn unit
- Calculating Fluid resucitation (www.burn-app.com)
- Antibiotics administration
- Procedure: Cleaning the burn (step-by-step)
- Procedure: Applying bandages (step-by-step)

- Face
- Arm
- Hands
- Thorax
- Leg
- Foot

- Using Aquacel burn
- Using flamazine/silverderma and jelonet

- Procedure: Surgical debridement (necrectomy)
- Procedure: Skin grafting
- Post-operative care
- Follow-up treatment

- Evaluating Burns

- Procedure: Changing the bandage

- **The topic: Facial flaps (the design of the chapter) is:**

- Vascular supply

- Designing af local skin flap

- Patient history and presentation
- Pre-operative work-up
- Procedures:
- Rotation flap

- Introduction
- Definitions
- Design
- Flap proportions
- Cases

- Interpolated flap

- etc

- Etc
- Post-operative care

**The topic: MM**

- Background and Definitions
- Patophysiology (Skin anatomy)
- Diagnosis

- Prognostic factors
- ABCDE rule
- Patient history and presentation

- Types of Melanoma

- SSMM with photo
- Nodular MM with photo
- etc

- TNM staging
- Prognosis
- Pre-operative work-up
- Procedure

- Excision of MM step-by-step
- Re-exc of MM step-by-step

- Indication
- Pre-operative considerations
- step-by-step photos
- post-operative care
- Pearls and Pitfalls

- Sentinel node

- etc

- Axillary lymph node dissection
- Groin lymph node dissection
- Neck lymph node dissection

- Histopathologic description of MM
- Follow-up regimen in Denmark

- Follow-up algorithm

- Follow-up consultation

- Adjuvant therapy

**The Topic: Massive Weightloss**

- Introduction with background and definitions
- Anatomy
- Patophysiology of massive weightloss (Following gastric bypass or change in dietary and physical activity)
- The referral
- Indications and Contraindications
- Brachioplasty

- Introduction
- Patient history and presentation
- Preoperative considerations
- Procedure (step-by-step)
- Post-operative
- Cases 1-2-3-4

- Abdominoplasty

- etc

- Fleur de lis (vertical abdominoplasty)
- 360 Belt lipoectomy
- Thigh plasty
- Mastopexia (LOPOSAM – Lower pole subglandular advancement mastoplasty)

## 5. Indications and Contraindications

Structure of the indication and contraindication page:

- **Authors**
- **Indications** for surgery in the specific diagnosis/topic/procedure.
- **Who and when** to operate?
- **Contraindication** including comorbidities or other factors that makes patients unsuitable for this procedure.
- **References**

### Examples

- Indication for treatment of gynocomastia, SCC etc.
- Indication for a bilobar nasal flap instead of a nasolabial flap.
- Indication for a TAP flap instead of a DIEP flap in breast reconstruction.

## 6. Drop-down menu with procedure and cases

Procedure and cases must be placed in a drop-down menu, where the menu item has the name of the procedure and the procedure page is titled “Procedure”, see the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/). How cases are named is described in the section below called “Cases”.

Structure of procedure and case pages:

- **Authors**
- **Introduction to the step-by-step case**

- *Short and precise patient history *

- Age
- Sex
- Reason for admission
- Location of tumor/reconstruction/etc
- E.g: “51-year old female admitted to Odense University Hospital for delayed breast reconstruction with a Thoracodorsal Artery Perforator flap (TAP flap).”

- Patient Examination

- Inspection

- Palpation
- Function of relevant body parts, arteria, nerves
- E.g: “Inspection: Right breast with horizontal mastectomy scar. Palpation: Tight scaring with skin adhesion to the thoracic wall. Function: Normal function of arm. No lymphedema. Appropriate amount of excess skin to raise a TAP flap. Sufficient perforators found on ultrasound.”

- **Pre-operative considerations**

- Anatomy, dissection plane, nerve, and arterial supply, etc.
- Flap design, dimensions, and thoughts on e.g. pedicle
- Useful tips for young doctors to prepare
- Pre-operative information to the patient on e.g. damage to the facial nerve

- **Before and after photo**
- **Step-by-step procedure** **photos**

- With number, description, and photos.

- Should be descriptive enough to be reproducible

- **Post-operative care**
- **Pearls**

- What are the advantages of this procedure/technique?

- **Pitfalls**

- What is the most complicated part of the surgery?

- **Video **

- If we have any of this procedure

- **References used in this procedure**

- Are numbered in the text: “(1)”, “(2)”, etc
- Book chapters and articles from peer-reviewed journals.
- Links to articles
- Links to web-sites

### Examples of procedures

- The Orlando Technique
- Bilobar flap for nasal reconstruction
- Excision of MM
- Sentinel node procedure
- Excision of tumor on the lip
- DIEP flap
- Primary assessment of burns patients
- Primary treatment of burns patients
- Breast reduction

### Cases

Cases are created and placed under the same menu item as the procedure. Then they will automatically be displayed at the bottom of the procedure or case.

Cases should have a title in the following format: “Case [number]: [description]” e.g. “Case 1: Hypertrophic breast”. It is important to use a colon “:”.

An example of a case could be breast lift using the Orlando Technique (including use of wise pattern and supero-medial stilk). In the future we will have several cases of the same procedure.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/table-of-content
TITEL: Table of content

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Table of content

A table of content can be useful to help users navigate a long page. On PlastSurgeon the table of content is shown on the right-hand side.

- A table of content is always shown on the Procedure and Case pages.
- A table of content can be enabled on a [Resource page](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/ressource-pages-vs-procedure-and-case-pages/) if you select the template “Topic – Resource page – With table of content”.
- The table of content automatically uses headings H1 and H2.

If you wish to see an example of table of content, then go to the [Anatomy](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/anatomy/) page in the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/) topic.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-20-kl.-10.55.23.png?resize=854%2C694&ssl=1)

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/image
TITEL: Image

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Image

Use the following guidelines for images:

- **Landscape format:** Use and take photos in landscape format, see figure 1.  This will enable the user to see more of the page as they are looking at the photo. If you have a photo in portrait consider using the guide: [From portrait to landscape format](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/change-photo-from-portrait-to-landscape-format/).
- **Full resolution: **Upload the photo in full resolution, if it is an illustration, then make it as large as possible, preferably around 2000-4000px in width and height.
- **Full width:** Let photos and illustrations be full width. This will them easier for the user to see, and it will create a consistent look with aligned left and right margins.
- **Watermark:** Upload without a watermark. WordPress will automatically add a watermark to the image, see figure 2.
- **Rectangle:** Illustrations should be uploaded as a rectangle. WordPress will present the image with rounded corners.
- **Stroke:** If an illustration has a white background and the subject of the illustration is cut off, then it often helps to add a stroke around it, to make it feel part of the content as a whole. There is a guide that shows you how: [Add a stroke to an image](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/add-a-stroke-to-an-image/).

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Portrait-vs.-landscape-1024x740.png?resize=1024%2C740&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Take and use photos in landscape mode

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-24-kl.-11.33.09-1024x766.png?resize=1024%2C766&ssl=1)Figure 2 – Image with watermark

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/be-aware-of-multi-level-list
TITEL: Be aware of multi-level lists

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Be aware of multi-level lists

Users on the internet scan for information. Pages with multi-level lists can be daunting and can make pages harder to scan. So consider some alternatives when it makes sense. Below is a multi-level list followed by two alternative ways to format the same content.

### Multi-level list

- Chemotherapy

- Epirubicin concomitant with cyclophosphamide followed by
- Docetaxel or Paclitaxel

- Endocrine therapy (adjuvant hormone therapy)

- Tamoxifen
- Aromatase inhibitors

- Targeted therapy

- Trastuzumab (Herceptin)

- Radiotherapy

### Alternative 1

- **Chemotherapy:** Epirubicin concomitant with cyclophosphamide followed by Docetaxel or Paclitaxel
- **Endocrine therapy** (adjuvant hormone therapy): Tamoxifen, Aromatase inhibitors
- **Targeted therapy**: Trastuzumab (Herceptin)
- **Radiotherapy**

### Alternative 2

**Chemotherapy** | Epirubicin concomitant with cyclophosphamide followed by
Docetaxel or Paclitaxel
**Endocrine therapy** (adjuvant hormone therapy) | Tamoxifen
Aromatase inhibitors
**Targeted therapy** | Trastuzumab (Herceptin)
**Radiotherapy** |

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/use-of-templates
TITEL: Use of templates

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Use of templates

Templates control how a page is presented. In some of the following guides, you will learn how to select the templates, but for now, it is just important to understand, that they exist.

In a topic, you can choose between the following five templates:

- “**Topic – Overview**“: Use as the parent page for the rest of the topic’s pages.
- “**Topic – Resource page – Without table of content”:** Use for [resource pages](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/ressource-pages-vs-procedure-and-case-pages/) when you wish to have a [table of content](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/table-of-content/) shown on the right-hand side.
- “**Topic – Resource page – With table of content**“: Use for [resource pages](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/ressource-pages-vs-procedure-and-case-pages/) when you do not wish to have a [table of content](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/table-of-content/) shown on the right-hand side.
- “**Topic – Menu item**“: Use for a menu item. There is no content on the page.
- “**Topic – Procedure and case”:** Used for step-by-step walkthrough of an operation.

In the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/) topic, you can see all templates in use. Figure 1 shows where to see each template.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Template-usage-1.png?resize=1024%2C861&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Example of templates in use

Figure 2 shows the administration panel, for the example topic.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Template-usage-Admin-1024x657.png?resize=1024%2C657&ssl=1)Figure 2 – Example of templates in the administration panel

TITEL: How to add a block

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# How to add a block

A WordPress page is build using blocks of content. To add a block make a new line, click on the plus-button and pick the block you want to add. If the block you wish to add is not present among the six suggestions, then search for the block you wish to add or click “browse all”.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-19-kl.-15.48.22.png?resize=648%2C702&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Add a block by searching for a block’s name or press “Browse all”

## Example

If you want to add the Step block, then make a new line, select the plus button, type “step” in the search input field, and select the “Step” block.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/Skaermbillede-2020-12-09-kl.-16.30.40.png?resize=712%2C492&ssl=1)

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/ressource-pages-vs-procedure-and-case-pages
TITEL: Page layout and templates

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Page layout and templates

In terms of layout and presentation, there are two types of pages on PlastSurgeon: The “Resource page”-layout and the “Procedure and case page”-layout.

- **The “Resource page”-layout** is used for free format pages. They can be used for any type of information. You will use them for e.g. introduction, anatomy, and other subtopics pages.
- **The “Procedure and case page”-layout** is used only for a step-by-step walkthrough of an operation, so you will use them only for procedure and case pages.

### Examples

If you want to see examples of the two types of page-layout you can go to the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/) topic.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Two-types-of-pages-1024x861.png?resize=1024%2C861&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Examples of the two types of pages

# Templates

Selecting a template for a page is a way to control, how the page is laid out, and how it works together with other pages. It adds functionality to the page, so it is important to select the right template for the right type of page.

In the guidelines about how to use the administration dashboard, it is described how to select a template for a page.

Most of your pages will contain content, but some pages will exist only for navigation purposes. In the list below, you can see an overview of all template names and their use:

- “**Topic – Overview**“: Use as the parent page for the rest of the topic’s pages.
- “**Topic – Resource page – Without table of content”:** Use for resource pages when you wish to have a [table of content](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/table-of-content/) shown on the right-hand side.
- “**Topic – Resource page – With table of content**“: Use for resource pages when you do not wish to have a [table of content](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/table-of-content/) shown on the right-hand side.
- “**Topic – Menu item**“: Use for a menu item. There is no content on the page.
- “**Topic – Procedure and case”:** Used for step-by-step walkthrough of an operation.

In the [Example](https://plastsurgeon.com/example/) topic, you can see all templates in use. Figure 1 shows where to see each template.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Template-usage-1.png?resize=1024%2C861&ssl=1)Figure 1 – Example of templates in use

Figure 2 shows the administration panel, for the example topic.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Template-usage-Admin-1024x657.png?resize=1024%2C657&ssl=1)Figure 2 – Example of templates in the administration panel

# Use of blocks

Pages are build using [blocks](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/how-to-add-a-block/) of content. To keep the pages in a consistent layout and format, the two types of pages are restricted to use only a few types of [blocks](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/how-to-add-a-block/) only.

### Ressource pages

Ressource pages use only the following [blocks](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/how-to-add-a-block/):

- “Heading” H1, H2, and H3
- “Paragraph”
- “Image”
- “List”
- “Table”
- “Gallery”
- PlastSurgeon “Link button”

### Procedure and case pages

Procedure and case pages use only the following [blocks](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/how-to-add-a-block/):

- “Paragraph”
- PlastSurgeon “Before and after”
- PlastSurgeon “Step”
- PlastSurgeon “Pearls”
- PlastSurgeon “Pitfalls”
- PlastSurgeon “Video”
- PlastSurgeon “References”

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/change-photo-from-portrait-to-landscape-format
TITEL: Portrait to landscape format

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Portrait to landscape format

Use this guide to change a photo from portrait to landscape format with a blurred background.

- Download [Adobe XD](https://www.adobe.com/products/xd.html) for free
- Create an artboard in landscape format. E.g. by typing in the width and height in the “Custom Size” fields on the welcome page.
- Drag your photo into the artboard.
- Duplicate it
- Select the photo in the back and scale it up in size so it covers the artboard.
- While the photo is selected select object blur in the right panel. Set the blur to 50.
- Select the artboard. Go to File > Export  > Selected. Press save.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/handbook/guidelines/add-a-procedure-or-case
TITEL: Add a procedure or case

*Kapitelsti: guidelines. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Add a procedure or case

In this guide, you will learn to add a menu item and a procedure or case. If you already have your menu in place and you just want to add a procedure or case, then jump to step 8.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.01.44.png?ssl=1)

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-16.05.33.png?ssl=1)

## Before and after

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-11.58.29.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)1

## Step 1: Go to “WP admin”

Click on the menu item “WP Admin” at the bottom of the side menu.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-12.00.19.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)2

## Step 2: Select “Pages”

Click on the menu item “Pages” in the side menu

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.04.44.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)3

## Step 3: Select “Add new”

The menu item is actually just a page, with a specific template. So go ahead and create a new page by selecting “Add new”.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.07.41.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)4

## Step 4: Add name of menu item

The title of the page is used as the name of the menu item, so add the menu item name in the title.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.22.26.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)5

## Step 5: Select template

Select the “Document” tab, then the “Page attributes” dropdown, and select the template called “Topic – Menu item”.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.22.26.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)6

## Step 6: Select a “Parent page” and “Order”

Now it’s time to place the page in the page hierarchy. Go to “Document” > “Page Attributes”. Select the parent page and then the order. The order controls in what order that pages are displayed in the menu. The pages are ordered from 0 and up.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-12-kl.-14.10.55.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)7

## Step 7: Save or publish

Save or publish the page

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.48.05.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)8

## Step 8: Add a new page

Now we want to add the Procedure or Case page. Create a new page by selecting “Add new”.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-15.52.18.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)9

## Step 9: Add title and content

Add a title and maybe some content. If it is a procedure then the title should be “Procedure”. If it is a case then the title should have the following format: “Case [number]: [Title of case]” e.g. “Case 1: Hypertrophic breasts”. Add the content in the following order and use [blocks](https://plastsurgeon.com/guidelines/how-to-add-a-block/) for all elements except Authors and Introduction.

- Authors (text in italic)
- Introduction (text)
- Before and After
- Steps
- Pearls (Optional)
- Pitfalls (Optional)
- Video (Optional)
- References

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-16.00.16.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)10

## Step 10: Select template

Select “Document”, then in the “Page attributes” dropdown and select the template “Topic – Procedure or case”

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-12-kl.-14.18.16-1.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)11

## Step 11: Select a “Parent page” and “Order”

Place the page in the page hierarchy. Select the parent page and then the order. The order controls in what order that pages are displayed in the menu. The pages are ordered from 0 and up.

- If you have followed this guide and created a menu item, then select the newly created menu item as the parent.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/Skaermbillede-2020-10-29-kl.-16.13.13.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)11

## Step 11: Add a featured image

The featured image is used when showing the procedure or case on the front page, the overview or in the bottom of procedure and cases.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Skaermbillede-2020-11-12-kl.-14.18.16.png?resize=1170%2C698&ssl=1)12

## Step 12: Save or publish

Save or publish the page.

TITEL: Introduction to Hidradenitis Suppurativa

*Kapitelsti: wound-management › hidradenitis-suppurativa. Indholdstype: handbook.*
# Introduction to Hidradenitis Suppurativa

Authors:* Miroslava Verbat, med. student, Ema Šutáková, med. student, Dominika Miklišová med. student, Julia Bartkova, MD*

## General Introduction

Hidradenitis suppurativa, also called Verneuil’s disease or acne inversa is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by lesions located in hair follicles (1).

It is described as a pyoderma of the adnexal structures, more specifically of the apocrine glands, located on the scalp, neck, axilla, breast, periumbilical, inguinal, perianal, and gluteal regions, creating fistulas, abscesses, and fibrosis.

The disease is not common, within Europe the prevalence is 1%.

Additionally, it is often misdiagnosed for folliculitis, acne vulgaris or cutaneous Crohn disease therefore delaying the accurate diagnosis up to years (2).

## Classification

(5) Hidradenitis suppurativa can be classified according to the severity of the lesions observed:

- **Hurley Stage I** (Mild): single or multiple isolated inflammatory nodule and abscesses formation, without sinus tracts and scarring.

- **Hurley Stage II** (Moderate): recurrent abscesses with >1 sinus tracts and scarring, separated by intact skin. We can observe solitary or multiple lesions.

- **Hurley Stage III** (Severe):  multiple lesions with interconnected sinus tracts, coalescing into inflammatory plaques with severe scarring, and abscesses across the entire region.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/wp-media/plastsurgeon.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/Stages-of-hidradenitis-suppurativa.png?resize=803%2C800&ssl=1)Picture 1: Scheme showing various stages of hidradenitis suppurativa, from simple abscess around a hair follicle to tunnel formation and severe scarring.

## Etiology

The exact etiology of hidradenitis is not known, although we can describe multiple predisposing factors:

- Obesity

- Smoking

- Genetics, 1/3 of the patients have a positive family history

- Female sex

- Dysregulation of inflammatory pathways,

- Bacterial colonization (Staphylococcus Aureus infection)

- Drugs (lithium therapy, contraception with higher to progesterone to estrogen ratio and levonorgestrel intrauterine device)

- Others: seronegative arthritis, spondylarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, anemia, psoriasis and systemic lupus erythematosus.

Moreover, clinical observations in female patients have confirmed that hormonal changes like the menstrual cycle, endocrine disorders such as polycystic ovary syndrome PCOS, metabolic syndrome, influence flare ups (6). This plays an additional role for its management.

## Treatment

### Medical management:

- Topical lincosamide applied twice daily for 3 months on local lesions (abscesses, nodules and pustules) is the first line treatment for Hurley stage I.

- Resorchinol, a topical agent with keratolytic, antipruritic and anti-inflammatory qualities can be applied twice daily on active inflammatory lesions.

- Intralesional injections with corticosteroids can also be considered on solitary lesions.

- Tetracyclines (for 10 weeks) is the treatment of choice for more broadly spread Hurley stage I and II. Clindamycin and rifampin (for 10 weeks) can be preferred for more severe Hurley stage II which is unresponsive to tetracyclines.

- Carbapenems can give rapid improvement (although it is given often as neoadjuvant therapy for bridging surgery (6).

Due to the strong link between endocrine imbalances and hidradenitis suppuritiva, anti-androgenic therapy can be introduced (for example, hinylestradiol and cyproteronacetate (6).

- Retinoids such as acitretin can be used for a special subtype of hidradenitis with follicular phenotype.

- Adalimumab (a IgG1 monoclonal antibody specific for TNF alpha, sold under the name HUMIRA) 40 mg every 3 weeks, subcutaneous injections is recommended for high stages disease with severe, extensive sinus tract, fistula formation and sclerosis (7).

Most patients require adjuvant medical therapies (topical or systemic) to diminish the inflammation and surgical treatment (drainage of tense abscesses in acute scenarios for immediate pain relief) (3).

The British Association of Dermatologists guidelines for the management of HS recommend surgical treatment for recurrent and severe cases which are not responsive to oral antibiotics, acitretin, or adalimumab (4).

### Surgical Treatment

We can divide the surgical management of hidradenitis into 3 types:

- Incision and drainage – for rapid pain relief. It presents with a 100 % recurrence rate,

- Deroofing – preserving the floor allows for the epithelial cells from sweat glands and hair follicles remnants to quickly reepithelize and heal by secondary intention – only 27% of recurrence was observed,

- Excision – more invasive option aimed to remove the affected tissue in its integrity. We can further subdivide it into 1) Limited/local excision, 2) Wide excision, 3) Radical excision. The recurrence rate is between 22 and 13%

Various options are possible for closure of the wound:

- Sutures,

- Grafts, STSG (split thickness and full thickness skin grafts),

- Flaps (if vascular channels and nerves are exposed) – lateral thoracic flap, fasciocutaneous V-Y flap, Limberg flap, musculocutaneous flap and thoracodorsal artery perforator flap,

- Healing by secondary intention (the wound will be left to heal by itself).

The treatment option can vary according to the stage of the disease.

Even though extensive surgery is often considered as the best option to minimize recurrence, less invasive interventions using a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser (Nd:YAG) can be recommended for Hurley stage II and III disease, additionally CO2 laser or surgical deroofing can also be used if the lesions present fibrotic scarring and nodules.

As a preventive measure depilation can also be suggested (3).

Overall, hidradenitis is difficult to diagnose and often refractory to conventional treatment which make its treatment and management very challenging for clinicians. A multidisciplinary approach is necessary.

## References

1. M.A. García-Sánche. Verneuil’s disease: A case report and literature review. Mexican Journal of Gastroenterology. Published July 2015. Accessed April 2023. [http://www.revistagastroenterologiamexico.org/en-verneuil39s-disease-a-case-report-articulo-S2255534X15000377](http://www.revistagastroenterologiamexico.org/en-verneuil39s-disease-a-case-report-articulo-S2255534X15000377)

2. [Georgios Kokolakis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=Kokolakis+G&cauthor_id=32610312). Delayed Diagnosis of Hidradenitis Suppurativa and Its Effect on Patients and Healthcare System. Karger Journal. Published July 1 2020. Accessed May 2023.  [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32610312/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32610312/)

3. Ratnakar Shukla. Surgical Treatment in Hidradenitis Suppurativa. Journal of Clinical Medicine. Published May 2022. Accessed April 2023.  [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9101712/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9101712/)

4. J.R. Ingram. British Association of Dermatologists guidelines for the management of hidradenitis suppurativa (acne inversa). British Journal of Dermatology. Published in 2018. Accessed April 2023. [https://bdng.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/BAD-Guidelines.pdf](https://bdng.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/BAD-Guidelines.pdf)

5. [Victoria Amat- Samaranch](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20406223211055920#con1). New perspectives on the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa. Sage journals. Published November 23, 2021. Accessed April 2023. [https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20406223211055920](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20406223211055920)

6. Lennart Ocker. Current Medical and Surgical Treatment of Hidradenitis Suppurativa / A Comprehensive Review. Journal of Clinical Medicine. Published 6 December 2022. Accessed April 2023. [https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/jcm/jcm-11-07240/article_deploy/jcm-11-07240.pdf?version=1670329917](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/jcm/jcm-11-07240/article_deploy/jcm-11-07240.pdf?version=1670329917)

7. Ricardo Blanco, MD. Long-term Successful Adalimumab Therapy in Severe Hidradenitis Suppurativa. Jama Dermatology. Published May 2009. Accessed April 2023. [https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamadermatology/fullarticle/712030](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamadermatology/fullarticle/712030)

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-abdominoplasty/lessons/lesson_msw279l1_5cmkny
TITEL: Relevant anatomy

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-abdominoplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Relevant anatomy

###

### Layers of the abdominal wall

The fatty tissue of the abdominal wall is divided into a superficial and a deep layer by Scarpa’s fascia. The anterior superior iliac spinae and the umbilicus are anchoring sites for the fascia, providing structural support for the skin. Dissection should not go deeper than the deep fascia lining the abdominal muscles. Preservation of Scarpa’s fascia is believed to reduce the risk of seroma. Caution should be shown when dissecting close to the umbilicus to preserve the umbilical stalk containing the blood supply.

### Blood supply

The skin and fat of the abdominal wall is supplied by perforating branches and can be divided into three different zones, known as the Hugor zones.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw2do8q-iqbajc.png)In the surgical planning, prior surgery and scars must be considered as the regions dependent on the sacrificed blood supply may be devascularized. When performing an abdominoplasty, the cutaneous supply of zone I and a large part of zone II will be disrupted. The survival of the abdominal flap is thus dependent on blood supply from zone III. Any disruption of the blood supply may jeopardize flap survival and the outcome of the abdominoplasty.

### Nerve supply

The abdominal wall is innervated by branches of sensory and motoric nerves.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw2euqu-c8rdll.png)The groin area and medioventral part of the thighs are sensory innervated by the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves which are located approximately 2 finger widths below ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine). Disruption of these nerves will result in loss of sensation in this area.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-abdominoplasty/lessons/lesson_msw279l1_v8z3zl
TITEL: Step-by-step procedure

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-abdominoplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Step-by-step procedure

### Preoperative marking

** Video af optegning – både simpel abdominalplastik og fleur-de-lis* *

Markings of the simple horizontal abdominoplasty and the fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty differ as the vertical incision lines are marked preoperatively in the fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty. Otherwise, the procedure of preoperative marking is the same.

Marking with the patient in standing position:

- With vertical lines, mark the jugulum, the xiphoid process, the anterior midline, the midclavicular lines, and the midaxillary lines.

- Address the mons to the optimal position and mark a point about 6-8 cm above the anterior labia majora commissure (point A).

- Draw a horizontal line of approximately 4 cm on each side of point A (line A).

- Palpate and mark ASIS (anterior superior iliac crest) bilaterally (point B).

- Connect line A to point B (line B) while pushing the skin upwards.

Continue marking with the patient in supine position:

- Re-mark the xiphoid process.

- Markings of fleur-de-lis:

- Use pinch test to estimate and mark the correct amount of excess tissue that can be removed in vertical direction on either side of the midline from the xiphoid process to below the umbilicus.

- Connect the markings by vertical lines on either side.

- Check for symmetry on both sides.

- An estimated superior incision line can be marked if desired but will be re-evaluated during surgery.

- Address the hanging mons by fixing it to fascia

- Excise the umbilicus first to avoid damaging the umbilical blood supply

- Make sure the superior incision line corresponds to the amount of skin possible to excise before making the incision to remove the excessive skin completely

- Leave a thin layer of tissue above the abdominal wall muscle to avoid seroma

- Do not tie the sutures at the T-junction, as this area has the least blood supply

- Compromising the blood supply to the umbilicus

- Tightening the skin too much

- Leaving larger blood vessels unhandled

### Step by step – simple horizontal abdominoplasty

**1.	Incisions**

Perform an incision along the inferior incision line from ASIS to ASIS all the way down to Scarpa’s fascia. Do not yet incise the superior line.

**2.	Dissection of the umbilicus**

Mark the desired shape of the umbilicus. There are varying methods of creating a new umbilicus, one of the standards being a horizontal oval shape allowing gravity to pull the umbilicus downwards avoiding creation of a long and narrow umbilicus.

When marked, lift the umbilicus with two skin hooks and carefully make an incision through the skin around the umbilicus. Dissect the umbilical stalk down to the fascia while paying attention to the blood supply by leaving a fat pad around the stalk.

**3.	Dissection of the excessive skin**

Use the monopolar cauterizer to perform hemostasis concomitant to dissection in cranial direction creating a flap of skin and fat.

Dissect along Scarpa’s fascia leaving a thin layer of fatty tissue above the abdominal wall muscle. Pay attention when approaching the umbilicus. Continue in cranial direction until the xiphoid process is reached. Perform hemostasis simultaneously to dissection. Larger perforating blood vessels should be ligated to ensure hemostasis. Smaller blood vessels can be attended with a bipolar cautery.

**4.	Removal of excessive skin**

When the area marked for removal has been dissected along Scarpa’s fascia, the patient is placed in a flexed position. Make sure the superior incision line can reach the inferior incision by pulling the skin downwards. If it is too tight, draw a new incision line. When the superior incision line has been checked, perform the final incision, and remove the excessive skin.

**5.	Suturing **

If the mons needs to be addressed, do this initially by fixing it to the fascia at the desired height.

Afterwards the superior skin flap is reapproximated to the inferior incision and sutured in three layers: Scarpa’s fascia, subcutis and cutis. Scarpa’s fascia is closed with single absorbable sutures, subcutis with continuous absorbable sutures, and dermis with intracutaneous absorbable suture.

Place the drains before closing Scarpa’s fascia completely.

**6.	Placing the umbilicus **

The umbilicus should be placed at its natural position where the umbilical stalk is. For most patients this corresponds to a placement in line with the superior point of the iliac crest. Mark the area of the new umbilicus on the superior flap and perform sharp incision of skin and fat. The umbilicus is fixed at its new position in two to three suture layers.

**7.	Bandage**

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.

**8.	First postoperative day **

Objective assessment for any complications including hematoma, seroma, or dehiscence. Drains can be removed if less than 50 ml produced.

### Step by step – fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty

**1.	Dissection of the umbilicus**

Lift the umbilicus with two skin hooks and carefully make an incision through the skin around the umbilicus. Dissect the umbilical stalk down to the fascia while paying attention to the blood supply by leaving a fat pad around the stalk.

**2.	Markings**

Re-examine the preoperative vertical incision lines by pinch test using instruments (Backhaus Lice). If necessary, re-mark new incision lines allowing for skin closure without too much tightening.

**3.	Vertical incisions**

Perform sharp incision along the vertical incision lines through the dermis. Switch to monopolar cautery and dissect straight down to Scarpa’s fascia. Do not yet incise the superior horizontal line.

**4.	Dissection of the excessive skin**

Use the monopolar cauterizer to perform hemostasis concomitant to dissection in caudal direction starting from the xiphoid process.

Dissect along Scarpa’s fascia leaving a thin layer of fatty tissue above the abdominal wall muscle. Pay attention when approaching the umbilicus. Continue in caudal direction until the inferior incision line is reached. Perform hemostasis simultaneously to dissection. Larger perforating blood vessels should be ligated to ensure hemostasis. Smaller blood vessels can be attended with a bipolar cautery.

**5.	Horizontal inferior incision**

Perform sharp incision through the dermig alon the horizontal inferior incision line. Use a monopolar cautery to dissect down to Scarpa’s fascia creating to flaps of skin and fatty tissue.

**6.	Marking of horizontal superior incision line**

Pull the abdominal skin flaps in caudal direction to estimate the amount of excess skin. Mark a horizontal incision line. This will create a triangle flap of excessive tissue on both sides of the abdomen that can be removed. Do not yet remove the excessive skin flaps.

**7.	Vertical suturing **

If the mons needs to be addressed, do this initially by fixing it to the fascia at the desired height.

Starting vertically from the xiphoid process, the skin is closed in Scarpa’s fascia with single absorbable sutures.

**8.	Removal of excessive skin**

Afterward placing the sutures in the deepest layer, examine the need of removing further skin before resecting the two skin flaps. Sharp incision along the horizontal superior line and remove the two triangle flaps with monopolar cautery. Secure hemostasis with bipolar cautery and ligation if needed.

**9.	Horizontal suturing **

The superior skin flaps are reapproximated to the inferior line medially with a single absorbable suture in Scarpa’s fascia. Place single inverted absorbable sutures in Scarpa’s fascia horizontally. Place the drains before closing Scarpa’s fascia completely.

**10.	Final suturing **

The skin is sutured in three layers: Scarpa’s fascia, subcutis and cutis. Scarpa’s fascia is closed with single absorbable sutures, subcutis with continuous absorbable sutures, and dermis with intracutaneous absorbable suture.

**11.	Placing the umbilicus **

The umbilicus should be placed at its natural position where the umbilical stalk is. For most patients this corresponds to a placement in line with the superior point of the iliac crest. Mark the area of the new umbilicus on the superior flap and perform sharp incision of skin and fat. The umbilicus is fixed at its new position in two to three suture layers.

**12.	Bandage**

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.

**13.	First postoperative day **

Objective assessment for any complications including hematoma, seroma, or dehiscence. Drains can be removed if less than 50 ml produced.

### Postoperative

# What you will learn

Abdominoplasty is the general term for removal of excessive skin from the abdomen. It includes abdominoplasty as a horizontal procedure, a vertical procedure, or a combined procedure (ad modum fleur-de-lis). An abdominoplasty removing overhanging skin and fat (pannus) is known as a panniculectomy and is performed for medical reasons. In this chapter, we will cover the abdominoplasty only.

In order to receive abdominoplasty, depending on local guidelines, the patient needs to have excessive skin equalizing Danish scale grade 2 or 3 and experience and substantial skin difficulties such as infection and chafing.

# Introduction

A brachioplasty is a procedure removing excess skin of the upper arms.

In this chapter, we will address the examination and surgical technique for the brachioplasty.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty/lessons/lesson_msw3ryjv_aornqt
TITEL: Indications and operative considerations

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Indications and operative considerations

In order to receive brachioplasty, depending on local guidelines, the patient needs to have excessive skin equalizing Danish scale grade 2 or 3 and experience and substantial skin difficulties such as infection and chafing.

Skin excess is defined from the lower definition of the muscle and evaluated by pinch test with the arm elevated 90 degrees.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw3ya1b-3v4cx0.png)Bat-wing deformity is evident in both grade 2 and 3, marking a loose posterior axillary fold.

To differentiate between grade 2 and 3, the patient needs to be assessed with the arms in a 90 degrees abduction of both shoulders and elbows as shown in the FIGURE.

Liposuction should be considered to prevent bulking at the elbows enhancing the cosmetic outcome and to prepare a secure dissection plane avoiding crucial structures and seroma.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty/lessons/lesson_msw3s6l2_lr3izn
TITEL: Anatomy and structures in danger

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Anatomy and structures in danger

When performing brachioplasty including liposuction attention must be paid to vital structures of the axilla and to the nerves of the upper arm.

The axilla contains the axillary artery, cephalic vein, and brachial plexus. Special attention must also be paid to preserve lymphatic vessels, basilic vein and the following nerves:

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw3zw6t-eu2ww0.png)All three nerves are sensory nerves innervating the medial and posterior aspect of the arm. Injury of these cutaneous nerves may lead to changes in sensibility (paresthesia or dysesthesia) of the medial aspect of the arm. It is crucial to preserve these cutaneous nerves and leave the brachial fascia intact.

Liposuction creates a dissection plane avoiding crucial structures including nerves, subcutaneous vessels, and lymphatics.

The incision, and consequently the scar, should be placed at the posterior-medial of the arm.

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Preoperative marking

Placement of the scar can vary according to surgeon and patient preferences. In this chapter, medial scar placement is explained.

*Video af optegning*

*Skematisk tegning af incisionslinjer*

- Marking is done with the patient in standing position with the shoulder in 90-degrees abduction and elbow in 90-degrees flexion.

- Mark the medial intermuscular groove (line A). This will be the location of the scar.

- Using line A as a fixpoint perform downwards traction of the skin and mark the amount of excess skin along the line. Connect the marks with a horizontal superior incision line (line B).

- Then, using line A as a fixpoint perform upwards traction of the skin and mark the amount of excess skin along the line. Connect the marks with a horizontal inferior incision line (line C).

- Connect the superior line to the inferior line near the medial epicondyle.

- The incision line can be extended in the axilla with a fishtail incision to remove excess skin along the lateral chest wall.

- Use pinch test to evaluate the incision lines.

- Add vertical lines to ease skin closure after removal of the excess skin.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty/lessons/lesson_msw3sq6g_l0ysln
TITEL: Step-by-step procedure

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massie-weight-loss-brachioplasty. Indholdstype: document.*
# Step-by-step procedure

**1.	Liposuction**

Superficial liposuction is performed within the marked area removing the superficial fat compartment between the skin and the aponeurosis. Special attention should be paid when performing liposuction near the axilla.

**2.	Incision**

Sharp incision only through the skin along the inferior incision line. Leave the superior incision intact.

**3.	Dissection **

With monopolar cautery dissect along the spatium created by liposuction constantly keeping a firm pull on the skin creating a flap of skin. If dissected along the correct level, the subcutaneous vessels, lymphatics, and nerves are preserved, and bleeding is avoided.

**4.	Final incision **

Pull the inferior line upwards while pulling the skin flap downwards and evaluate the amount of tissue marked for excision. If needed, correct the superior incision line. When ultimate superior line has been marked, perform sharp incision through the skin and remove the skin flap.

**5.	Suturing **

The skin is closed in three layers: the superficial fascia, dermis, and the skin.

The fascia is approximated with absorbable inverted sutures using the vertical guide lines. Start by fixating the corner of the axilla. The dermis by absorbable running suture, and the skin with absorbable intracutaneous suture.

**6.	Bandage **

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.

**7.	First postoperative day **

Objective assessment for any complications including hematoma, seroma, or dehiscence.

- Use liposuction to create a safe spatium for dissection protecting neurovascular bundles

- Address the excess skin of the lateral chest wall by prolonging the incision with a fish tail incision

- Consider scar placement preoperatively – medial (brachial groove) or posterior placement

- Over-aggressive removal of skin resulting in prolonged wound healing, widened and hypertrophic scars, and higher risk of dehiscence

- Critical structures of the axilla and medial arm including nerves, vascular and lymphatic structures

# Introduction

A belt lipectomy is the term for a combined circumferential procedure of an abdominoplasty and lower back lift, also known as a 360 degrees plasty.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy/lessons/lesson_msw34jht_gak6dq
TITEL: Indications and operative considerations

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy. Indholdstype: document.*
# Indications and operative considerations

The general indications and contraindications when performing MWL-surgery will be addressed in another chapter. Follow this link to read more: ***link ***

### Procedure specific indications

In general, third-degree patients are candidates to belt lipectomy. Regarding belt lipectomy the classifications are as followed:

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw35eo2-odwbir.png)An abdomen with grade 3 pannus extending posteriorly to the mid-axillary line should be considered for a belt lipectomy.

Belt lipectomy could also be considered for an abdomen with a grade 2 pannus if moderate or severe grades of the lower back is found. The lower trunk regions are adjacent making a circumferential procedure desirable in order to address both ventral and posterior trunk sagging and skin excess. As a rule of thumb, a grade 2 abdomen and a grade 2 lower back equals 4 outnumbering a grade 3 and thereby suggesting a circumferential procedure [1].

### Procedure specific contraindications

If the patient is planning on becoming pregnant in the future.

**References**

- Berg JO, Rosenkrantz Hölmich L, Printzlau A. The Danish Scale for visual rating of massive weight loss body contours. Conceptualization and construct. J Plast Surg Hand Surg. 2019;53(4):189–197. doi:10.1080/2000656X.2019.1581790

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy/lessons/lesson_msw3bbh0_7rd5xo
TITEL: Preoperative marking
FORFATTERE: Tegning af incisionslinjer til simpel abdominalplastik og fleur-de-lis

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy. Indholdstype: document.*
# Preoperative marking

### Preoperative marking of the abdomen

*Tegning af incisionslinjer til simpel abdominalplastik og fleur-de-lis*

Simple horizontal abdominoplasty is explained in this chapter. For fleur-de-lis abdominoplasty, please read this chapter "Abdominoplasty"*.*

Marking with the patient in standing position:

- With vertical lines, mark the jugulum, the xiphoid process, the anterior midline, the midclavicular lines, and the midaxillary lines.

- Address the mons to the optimal position and mark a point about 6-8 cm above the anterior labia majora commissure (point A).

- Draw a horizontal line of approximately 4 cm on each side of point A (line A).

- Palpate and mark ASIS (anterior superior iliac crest) bilaterally (point B).

- Connect line A to point B (line B) while pushing the skin upwards.

Continue marking with the patient in supine position:

- Re-mark the xiphoid process.

- An estimated superior incision line can be marked if desired but will be re-evaluated during surgery.

### Preoperative marking of the lower back

*Skematisk tegning af incisionslinjer*

- Marking is done with the patient in standing position.

- With vertical lines, mark the midline (line A), midaxillary lines (line B), and a line at the lateral border of the nates bilaterally (line C).

- By palpation, mark the iliac crest on line B (point A). Perform pinch test to determine the amount of excess skin to remove and mark this point (point B) bilaterally.

- Mark a fixed point about 4 cm above the intergluteal cleft (point C).

- Connect points B and C with a slightly curved line (inferior incision line). Connect the dorsal inferior incision line to the ventral inferior incision line laterally.

- By pinch test determine the amount of excess skin from midline to iliac crest and mark it with dots. Connect the dots to mark the superior incision line.

- Using the midline, measure a fixed point and draw vertically lines on both sides. Use the fixpoints to check if the distance between the inferior and superior markings are symmetrical on both sides.

- After the superior and inferior lines have been marked, ask the patient to bend forward and re-do the pinch test. Adjust the markings if necessary to prevent over-correction.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy/lessons/lesson_msw3bfsv_x8u16t
TITEL: Step-by-step procedure

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-belt-lipectomy. Indholdstype: document.*
# Step-by-step procedure

The circumferential procedure is started on the lower back with the patient in prone position.

### Prone position

**1.	Markings **

Re-examine the preoperative markings by pinch test using instruments (Backhaus Lice). If necessary, re-mark a new superior incision line allowing for skin closure without too much tightening.

**2.	Incisions**

Perform sharp incision through dermis along the inferior and superior incision lines. Switch to monopolar to dissect straight down to the deep fascia.

**3.	Dissection of the excessive skin**

Use the monopolar cauterizer to perform hemostasis concomitant to dissection. When the deep fascia is reached, follow the fascia medially in lateral direction creating a flap of skin and fat.

Perform hemostasis simultaneously to dissection. Larger perforating blood vessels should be ligated to ensure hemostasis. Smaller blood vessels can be attended with a bipolar cautery.

**4.	Suturing **

The superior skin flap is reapproximated to the inferior incision and sutured in three layers: Scarpa’s fascia, subcutis and cutis. Scarpa’s fascia is closed with single inverted absorbable sutures, subcutis with continuous absorbable sutures, and dermis with intracutaneous absorbable suture. Leave a length of around 5 cm in each lateral end without sutures. The skin of each lateral end is closed with staples allowing for ventral continuation of the incision.

**5.	Bandage**

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.
Apply temporary Tegaderm to the lateral ends.

The patient is then peroperatively turned to supine position to continue the circumferential procedure on the abdomen.

### Supine position

**1.	Dissection of the umbilicus**

Mark the desired shape of the umbilicus. There are varying methods of creating a new umbilicus, one of the standards being a horizontal oval shape allowing gravity to pull the umbilicus downwards avoiding creating a long and narrow umbilicus.

When marked, lift up the umbilicus with two skin hooks and carefully make an incision all the way through the skin around the umbilicus. Dissect the umbilical stalk all the way down to the fascia while paying attention to the blood supply by leaving a fat pad around the stalk.

**2.	Remove staples **

Remove the Tegaderm and staples at each lateral end.

**3.	Incisions**

Perform an incision along the inferior incision line from ASIS to ASIS all the way down to Scarpa’s fascia. Do not yet incise the superior line.

**4.	Dissection of the excessive skin**

Use the monopolar cauterizer to perform hemostasis concomitant to dissection in cranial direction creating a flap of skin and fat.

Dissect along Scarpa’s fascia leaving a thin layer of fatty tissue above the abdominal wall muscle. Pay attention when approaching the umbilicus. Continue in cranial direction until the xiphoid process is reached. Perform hemostasis simultaneously to dissection. Larger perforating blood vessels should be ligated to ensure hemostasis. Smaller blood vessels can be attended with a bipolar cautery.

**5.	Removal of excessive skin**

When the area marked for removal has been dissected along Scarpa’s fascia, the patient is placed in a flexed position. While pulling the superior skin flap downwards to the inferior incision line, mark the superior incision line connecting it to the lateral incisions from the lower back lift. When the superior incision line has been checked, perform the final incision, and remove the excessive skin.

**6.	Suturing **

If the mons needs to be addressed, do this initially by fixing it to the fascia at the desired height.

Afterwards the superior skin flap is reapproximated to the inferior incision and sutured in three layers: Scarpa’s fascia, subcutis and cutis. Scarpa’s fascia is closed with single absorbable sutures, subcutis with continuous absorbable sutures, and dermis with intracutaneous absorbable suture.

Place the drains before closing Scarpa’s fascia completely.

**7.	Placing the umbilicus **

The umbilicus should be placed at its natural position where the umbilical stalk is. For most patients this corresponds to a placement in line with the superior point of the iliac crest. Mark the area of the new umbilicus on the superior flap and perform sharp incision of skin and fat. The umbilicus is fixed at its new position in two to three suture layers.

**8.	Bandage**

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.

**9.	First postoperative day **

Objective assessment for any complications including hematoma, seroma, or dehiscence. Drains can be removed if less than 50 ml produced.

# Massive Weight Loss - Introduction

This course explores the principles of plastic surgery after massive weight loss. It will cover topics such as the benefits of plastic surgery for patients who have lost a significant amount of weight, the types of procedures that may be necessary to achieve the desired outcome, the potential risks associated with these procedures, and the post-operative care and recovery process. It will also discuss the psychological impact of massive weight loss and the importance of multidisciplinary care. Through lectures, case studies, and hands-on experience, participants will gain a comprehensive understanding of the plastic surgery process and its implications for massive weight loss patients.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw1hsl6_97naz0
TITEL: Pathophysiology of Excess Skin

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Pathophysiology of Excess Skin

The mechanism behind excessive and hanging loose skin is not completely known, but several theories are currently being tested. From what is known, obesity causes stretching of the skin leading to significant changes in the skin structure over time. This includes an impact on collagen and elastin fibers resulting in loss of skin elasticity, increased fibrosis, decreased vascular proliferation, and formation of striae and stretch marks. After MWL, the ability of the skin to retract is affected leading to skin excess and laxity.

Other factors presumed to impact skin structure and ability are amount and rate of weight loss, age, smoking, sun exposure, and genetic disposition [3].

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw1hsl6_gl5nr8
TITEL: What you will learn

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# What you will learn

After a massive weight loss (MWL), patients can experience varying degrees of excess skin most often on the abdomen, lower or upper back, upper arms, inner thighs, or breasts. The excess skin might be causing various physical and psychological discomforts and reduced physical activity. These complications can have a severe impact on the patient’s life. Removal of the excess skin may have an ameliorating effect on these challenges resulting in higher mobility, overall health, cosmetics, and quality of life.

An estimate of one third of all patients undergoing MWL will require removal of excess skin [1]. Whether skin removal is performed at public hospitals depends on the grade of excess skin and the subjective complaints.

In the following chapters we address the examination of the MWL-patient and the surgical techniques used on the abdomen, back, arms, and thighs. Techniques used on the breast when performing mastopexy (breast lift) will be addressed in the chapter "breast surgery".

**References**

1.	Hurwitz DJ, Ayeni O. Body contouring surgery in the massive weight loss patient. Surg Clin North Am. 2016;86(4):875-85. doi:10.1016/j.suc.2016.03.011

2.	Berg JO, Rosenkrantz Hölmich L, Printzlau A. The Danish Scale for visual rating of massive weight loss body contours. Conceptualization and construct. J Plast Surg Hand Surg. 2019;53(4):189–197. doi:10.1080/2000656X.2019.1581790

3.	Hany M, Zidan A, Ghozlan NA et al. Comparison of Histological Skin Changes After Massive Weight Loss in Post-bariatric and Non-bariatric Patients. Obes Surg. 2024;34, 855–865. doi: 10.1007/s11695-024-07066-y

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw1hsl6_li9h7k
TITEL: Clinical Symptoms and Patient Impact

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Clinical Symptoms and Patient Impact

Patients suffering from excess skin might experience a long list of functional, cosmetic, and psychosocial challenges. Functional challenges include but are not limited to skin entrapment, skin chafing, intertrigo and infection in skin folds, odor nuisance, impaired physical activity especially from pain and pulling of skin folds, sanitary difficulties, and pain in the ischial region due to the loss of cushioning fat pads. Psychosocial challenges might include social concerns, altered psychological self-acceptance, lower quality of life, and problems being intimate with a partner.

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw1hsl6_vb2vag
TITEL: Surgical interventions

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Surgical interventions

Surgical removal of excess skin is divided into different procedures. Most often, only one procedure will be performed at a time requiring several separate procedures done over a longer time period.

**Abdominoplasty:** Excision of excess skin on the abdomen in horizontal and/or vertical direction and/or reposition of mons pubis.

**Lower body lift:** Excision of excess skin of the lower back and nates.

**Belt lipectomy: **Combination of abdominoplasty and lower body lift. Also known as a 360-degree procedure.

**Upper body lift: **Excision of excess skin on the upper back. Can be extended as a circular procedure including mastopexy.

**Brachioplasty:** Excision of excess skin on the upper arms.

**Thighplasty:** Excision of excess skin on the inner thighs in vertical and/or horizontal direction.

**References **

1.	Sundhedsstyrelsen, Sygehuse og Beredskab Plastikkirurgisk korrektion efter massivt vægttab. Faglig visitationsretningslinje København: Sundhedsstyrelsen, Sygehuse og Beredskab, 2013. ISBN: 978-87-7104-591-8

2.	Garoosi K, Mundra L, Jabbari K et al. Aesthet Surg J Open Forum. 2023;31(5):ojad080. doi: 10.1093/asjof/ojad080

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw1hsl6_w2vb6r
TITEL: Definitions

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Definitions

In Denmark, MWL is defined by the loss of ≥15 BMI points and stable weight for ≥6 months. Calculation is performed comparing the patient’s maximum weight (non-pregnant) to the current weight. MWL is not defined by weight loss method.

The Danish Scale (DS) is a visual rating scale used to assess body contour deformities and excessive skin in female patients [2]. Grade 1 is defined as light changes of cosmetic character, grade 2 as moderate changes requiring simple procedures, and grade 3 as severe changes requiring major or circular procedures.

---
## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw222cn_woixvq
TITEL: Risks and Complications

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Risks and Complications

Complications span from mild to severe requiring surgical intervention. Patients should always be informed about risks and complications including bleeding, infection, hematoma, seroma, wound rupture, scar deformity, skin or fat necrosis, and thrombosis. Furthermore, the skin can loosen within months-years post-surgery requiring re-operation of the area.

Higher risk of complications is seen in patients with malnutrition, high BMI, or active smoking status [2]. Therefore, it is critical that the patient meet the criteria of BMI ≤30, metabolic stability, and non-smoking status. Post-bariatric patients are known to have a higher incidence of complications compared to patients achieving a MWL by lifestyle changes, partly due to malabsorption [3].

Complications are seen in around 30% of all cases, seroma and wound dehiscence being the most frequent type of complications, and abdominoplasty being the procedure associated with the highest risk of complications [4].

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-introduction/lessons/lesson_msw226ub_xntnlf
TITEL: Preoperative preparation

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-introduction. Indholdstype: document.*
# Preoperative preparation

All MWL patients should be prepared for surgery by the following:

**Patient history**

- Maximum weight (outside pregnancy), current weight and decrease in BMI points

- Cause of weight loss: bariatric surgery or lifestyle changes

- Number of pregnancies and birth method (cesarian section), previous surgery (scars)

- Any mechanical issues during sports or other physical activities

**Objective assessment and ordinations**

- MWL blood samples (mentioned in this chapter (link til “Surgical intervention”))

- St.c. et p.

- ECG: >60 years of age or known heart disease/symptoms of heart disease

- Anesthesiologic evaluation to ensure patient is fit for general anesthesia

- Stabilize co-morbidities, e.g. diabetes

- Blood thinners: Consider the need for pause, bridging, INR monitoring. In Denmark, Regulations from The Danish Society of Thrombosis and Hemostasis are used ([https://www.dsth.dk/bridging2018/index.html](https://www.dsth.dk/bridging2018/index.html))

- Assess the venous thromboembolism risk by calculating the Caprini score of the patient: [https://www.mdcalc.com/caprini-score-venous-thromboembolism-2005](https://www.mdcalc.com/caprini-score-venous-thromboembolism-2005)

- Prophylactic antibiotics

To differentiate between grade 2 and 3, the patient needs to be assessed in flank view as shown in the figure.

# Introduction

A lower back lift covers removal of excessive skin from the lower back due to buttock changes including flattening/volume loss of the buttocks and sagging of the infra-gluteal fold. It may be combined with an autologous buttock augmentation to restore projection.

TITEL: Anatomy and structures in danger

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-lower-back-lift. Indholdstype: document.*
# Anatomy and structures in danger

### Layers of the posterior lower trunk

The lower back, or lumbar region, is divided into several regions: Vertebral, lumbar, sacral, and gluteal region. The fatty tissue of the lower back is divided into a superficial and a deep layer by the superficial fascia. The iliac crest and spinous processes of the vertebrae are anchoring sites for the deep fascia. Dissection should follow the deep fascia.

*Tegning af ryggens lag*

### Blood supply

The skin and fatty tissue of the lower and midback is supplied by dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries. The gluteal area is supplied by the superior and inferior arteries arising from the internal iliac artery.

**Tegning **

### Nerve supply

The skin of the lower back and nates is innervated in an organized dermatomal pattern by dorsal branches of spinal nerves from corresponding spinal levels (L1-S5). The branches are the nn. clunium superiores, medii, and inferiores, and n. iliohypogastricus.

**Tegning **

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-lower-back-lift/lessons/lesson_msw2x146_no60ac
TITEL: Preoperative marking

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-lower-back-lift. Indholdstype: document.*
# Preoperative marking

### Preoperative marking

**Video af optegning* *

**Skematisk tegning af incisionslinjer **

- Marking is done with the patient in standing position.

- With vertical lines, mark the midline (line A), midaxillary lines (line B), and a line at the lateral border of the nates bilaterally (line C).

- By palpation, mark the iliac crest on line B (point A). Perform pinch test to determine the amount of excess skin to remove and mark this point (point B) bilaterally.

- Mark a fixed point about 4 cm above the intergluteal cleft (point C).

- Connect points B and C with a slightly curved line (inferior incision line).

- By pinch test determine the amount of excess skin from midline to iliac crest and mark it with dots. Connect the dots to mark the superior incision line.

- Using the midline, measure a fixed point and draw vertically lines on both sides. Use the fixpoints to check if the distance between the inferior and superior markings are symmetrical on both sides.

- After the superior and inferior lines have been marked, ask the patient to bend forward and re-do the pinch test. Adjust the markings if necessary to prevent over-correction.

- Measure the amount of excess skin with the patient in upright and in bend position using the pinching method

- Preoperative markings on the back differentiate between men and women. A male patient typically prefers a scar that is linear and lower, while a female patient typically prefers a wing-shaped scar, which enhances the contour of the nates

- Autologous augmentation to restore volume loss

- Non-sufficient preoperative markings resulting in a prolonged gluteal cleft

- Removing too much skin resulting in over-tightening of the skin, prolonged wound healing, and higher risk of dehiscence

## KILDE: https://beta.plastsurgeon.com/courses/massive-weight-loss-lower-back-lift/lessons/lesson_msw2x7rn_cswqop
TITEL: Step-by-step procedure

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-lower-back-lift. Indholdstype: document.*
# Step-by-step procedure

### Step-by-step

**1. Markings**

Re-examine the preoperative markings by pinch test using instruments (Backhaus Lice). If necessary, re-mark a new superior incision line allowing for skin closure without too much tightening.

**2. Incisions**

Perform sharp incision through dermis along the inferior and superior incision lines. Switch to monopolar to dissect straight down to the deep fascia.

**3. Dissection of the excessive skin**

Use the monopolar cauterizer to perform hemostasis concomitant to dissection. When the deep fascia is reached, follow the fascia medially in lateral direction creating a flap of skin and fat.

Perform hemostasis simultaneously to dissection. Larger perforating blood vessels should be ligated to ensure hemostasis. Smaller blood vessels can be attended with a bipolar cautery.

**4. Suturing**

The superior skin flap is reapproximated to the inferior incision and sutured in three layers: Scarpa’s fascia, subcutis and cutis. Scarpa’s fascia is closed with single inverted absorbable sutures, subcutis with continuous absorbable sutures, and dermis with intracutaneous absorbable suture.

**5. Bandage**

Apply Micropore to all cicatrices.

**6. First postoperative day**

*Billede af patient på 1. POD*

Objective assessment for any complications including hematoma, seroma, or dehiscence.

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-upper-body-lift. Indholdstype: document.*
# Indications and operative considerations

In order to receive upper back lift, depending on local guidelines, the patient needs to have excessive skin equalizing Danish scale grade 2 and functional deficits or grade 3.

![](https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com/nordicsurgery/plastsurgeon/uploads/msw3mbxw-bhbp4r.png)To differentiate between grade 1 and 2, the patient needs to be assessed with the arms abducted. In grade 1, the skin excess is corrected, whereas in grade 2 the skin excess still shows (FIGURE).

As a rule of thumb, a grade 2 upper back and a grade 2 breast equals 4 and may indicate and benefit from a circumferential procedure. A grade 1 upper back and grade 2 breast equals 3 and may be treated satisfactory by an extended mastopexy, while grade 2 upper back and grade 1 breast may be treated satisfactory with a short upper body lift.

TITEL: Anatomy and structures in danger

*Kapitelsti: mwl › massive-weight-loss-upper-body-lift. Indholdstype: document.*
# Anatomy and structures in danger

### Layers of the posterior upper trunk

The upper back, or thoracic region, is divided into several regions: Vertebral, scapular, inter-, supra- and infrascapular region. The back has four main layers: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, deep fascia, superficial and deep muscles, and bone (ribs and columna). The subcutaneous tissue is divided into a superficial and a deep layer by the superficial fascia. The spinous processes of the vertebrae are anchoring sites for the deep fascia. Dissection should follow the deep fascia.

### Blood supply

The skin and fatty tissue of the upper back is supplied by dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries, perforating branches of the intercostal arteries, and subscapular artery.

### Nerve supply

The skin is innervated in an organized dermatomal pattern by dorsal branches of spinal nerves (rami dorsalis nervi spinalium) from corresponding spinal levels (T4-T9).

# Preoperative marking

Preoperative marking

*Video af optegning*

*Skematisk tegning af incisionslinjer*

- Marking is done with the patient in standing position and arms hanging along the side of the trunk.

- A horizontal superior incision line is marked (line A). This will be the location of the scar.

- Using line A as a fixpoint, mark the amount of excess skin by upwards traction of the skin. Connect the markings with a horizontal inferior incision line (line B).

- Evaluate the markings by pinch test.
